zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical checks used Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html . The scan-derived transcription and English review notes are this review’s work.

lines.note: Tōura denotes this shore or maritime place. The initial caron and the gloss’s printed Esta are retained without regularizing either form.
Tōsha denotes this kami shrine. Camis occurs inside the Portuguese explanation as the plural designation of the deities, rather than as another headword.
Tosha is vomiting and purging, explained by haki and kudasu. The comma after Vomitar and the terminal ca- are visible; camaras continues below.

runs.text: maras, como quãdo hũ eſtà doente de mordexim.

lines.note: Maras completes camaras, bowel evacuations. The comparison concerns a patient suffering from mordexim; the historical disease term is retained without imposing a modern diagnosis.
Tōshaku is a sparrow engaged in fighting, with tatakō suzume as its Japanese explanation. The circumflex on the headword differs visibly from the caron in tatacǒ.
The sparrow is entangled with another in combat. The repeated Tôxacu begins the proverb continued on the next physical row.
Hito ni ojizu completes the claim that the fighting sparrow does not fear people. The Portuguese starts its matching explanation; the close printed Opardal is retained.

runs.text: com outro pelejando não temegente. Aplicaſe

lines.note: The sparrow, caught up in fighting, does not fear people. Aplicaſe announces an application of the saying to human behaviour, continued below.

runs.text: ta nbem a homens que quando eſtão brigando não

lines.note: The saying also applies to men absorbed in a fight. The damaged opening is retained as ta nbem from the aligned draft: tambem is the clear intended word, but the missing stroke and unusual gap are not silently supplied.

runs.text: tem conta com ſenhor, nem com ninguem.

lines.note: The fighters pay no heed to their lord or anyone else. This completes the proverb’s human application, rather than introducing a separate maxim.
Tōsei denotes the present age, explained as the current world or present era. The attached Ataruyo spacing and the alternative marker l are preserved.

runs.text: de, ou eſte mundo de agora. ¶ Item, Cou

lines.note: De completes idade. The entry then adds the sense of something current now; Cou begins couſa without a securely visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ſa que corre agora de preſente.

lines.note: Completes couſa: something in current use at the present time. The short continuation belongs to the preceding Tǒxei entry.
Tosei is making one’s way through life, yo wo wataru. The example begins with roman To- after italic Vt; the OCR had incorrectly carried italics into the Japanese fragment.
Xei completes Toxei in the example tosei wo nageku. The Portuguese describes earning or managing one’s livelihood with hardship, with trabalhos divided at the line break.
Balhos completes trabalhos, followed by fadigas. The next example, tosei wo itonamu, begins on this row and continues below.
Mu completes itonamu. The Portuguese explains arranging one’s livelihood and sustenance; the divided Japanese verb remains in physical line order.
Tōsen is explained by an ascending mountain person, identified as xennin. The scan supports initial T, not OCR F; the description of a Chinese philosopher begins with Ho-.

runs.text: mem philosopho da China que viue nos mõtes,

lines.note: Mem completes homem. The Chinese philosopher lives in the mountains; philosopho is one printed word, correcting the OCR’s artificial division philoso pho.
These figures are said to perform wonders, including rising into the air. The visible i in marauilhas corrects the OCR omission without modernizing the historical u/v spelling.
Nos ares completes the claim of rising into the air. This short row closes the description of the mountain immortal.
This second Tôxen means combat or battle, explained by tatakai and tatakō. The broken capital is T, and the second explanatory form begins with lowercase t in the scan.
Tōsen here means a Chinese vessel, kara no fune. Its caron distinguishes it graphically from the two preceding circumflex-bearing entries.
Tōsendō is a road through mountains. The printed final caron and the historical Portuguese Estrada are preserved; the route’s direction is specified below.

runs.text: pera a parte do Leſte, em reſpeito de Miaco.

lines.note: The road runs eastward relative to Miaco, the capital. Miaco is a Japanese place designation embedded in a Portuguese sentence, so it is recorded for typeface review.
Tōset is explained as killing with a sword, katana de korosu. Catana is repeated within the Portuguese gloss; the final t of the headword is not expanded in the transcription.
The compound is explained as dying while fighting. The Portuguese morrer pelejando corresponds directly to tatakai shisuru rather than to the ordinary word for a year below.
Ou à eſpada adds death by the sword. This short continuation belongs to the battle-death entry.
Toshi means year. Toshi ga tsumoru, literally accumulating years, is glossed as growing old; the Portuguese infinitive is divided after En-.
Velhecer completes enuelhecer. Toshi ga takuru introduces advancing in age, with the Portuguese ir continued on the next line.
The first phrase completes growing in age. Toshi ga yuku supplies another expression for ageing, again followed by divided En-uelhecer.
After completing enuelhecer, the entry gives toshi wo koyuru or toru. These examples lead into passing from one year to another below.

runs.text: Paßar de hum anno a outro. ¶

lines.note: The gloss describes crossing from one year to another. Toshi no kure begins at the end of the row and continues across the physical break.
Re completes kure, the year’s end. A new example, toshi wo kurasu, then introduces living or passing one’s life.
The Portuguese glosses living or passing one’s life. Toshi wo okuru begins with the printed vo- segment, which continues below.
Curu completes okuru, passing the years. Toshi ga akuru then names the beginning of a new year, explained on the next row.
Começar o anno completes the example about the year beginning. Its brevity does not make it page furniture or an independent entry.
Tōshi is Chinese paper, explained as paper from Taitō. Both visible carons are retained; this is distinct from the preceding unmarked toshi “year.”
Toshibai, alternatively toshiubai, describes a person’s stage of life. Both printed forms remain distinct and the Portuguese emphasizes relative age.
Toshibai ga yoi describes being of a good or suitable age. The numerical illustration of that age continues below.
The example gives an age from thirty to forty and more. Enlargement shows a single grave stroke in tè, not the OCR tilde; Toxibaiga begins the next illustration.

runs.text: Paſſouſe ja aboa idade, ou he ja

lines.note: Sugita completes toshibai ga sugita, having passed the good age. The Portuguese says that the person is already old; the close aboa spacing is retained.
The previous gloss ends with velho. Toshibai ga wakai hito introduces a person still young, whose Portuguese description is continued below.
Ainda mancebo completes the young-person gloss. The short continuation is part of the same age example.

runs.text: O mais velho, ou de mais idade.

lines.note: Toshikasa denotes someone older or senior in age. The long s in the Japanese form is retained as printed.
Toshikasa no hito is the illustrative phrase for an older person, with Idem referring to the preceding definition. The visible pilcrow and capital T restore material lost or misread by OCR.
Toshikoro is an age or stage of life. The scan supports initial T and final Portuguese idade, correcting OCR r and idado.

runs.text: O paßar de hum anno à outro, ou

lines.note: Toshikoshi is passing from one year to another. The scan supports paßar, hum and anno, correcting the garbled OCR; the following lines explain two calendar occasions.

runs.text: ſair do inuerno, & entrar na prima vera, o

lines.note: The first description is leaving winter and entering spring. The final o belongs to o que acontece below, rather than the OCR’s additional alternative ou; prima vera remains printed as two words.

runs.text: que acontece na derradeira noite do Xiuaſu,

lines.note: The event occurs on the last night of Xiuaſu. The month name is Japanese embedded within Portuguese and is therefore a typeface-review term.

runs.text: que he a duodecima lũa, & no cabo, ou ter-

lines.note: Xiuaſu is identified as the twelfth lunar month. The gloss then turns to the end or limit of winter; termino is divided between ter- and mino.

runs.text: mino do inuerno, que às vezes ſe desencontra

lines.note: Mino completes termino. The text states that the winter endpoint sometimes does not coincide with the date explained in the next row.

runs.text: do derradeiro dia do Xiuaſu: estes dous tem-

lines.note: The comparison is with the last day of Xiuaſu. Tem- begins tempos on the next line; the baseline st spelling in estes is retained because the joined italic sorts do not justify overriding the provisional reading.

runs.text: pos chamão Rixxun que ſão duas maneiras de

lines.note: Pos completes tempos. The text calls these two occasions Rixxun and describes them as two ways of beginning the spring; the explanation is retained as the source states it.
Faru completes the explanation with the Japanese word for spring. It occurs inside the Portuguese sentence and is marked for optional typeface adjustment.

The gloss is “each year.” NINJAL identifies the corresponding entry as Toxidoxi, but this impression’s damaged fifth letter has the open shape of c and no secure ascender; the visible Toxicoxi is retained as a nonblocking textual caveat.
Toshihisashii means lasting many years. The scan’s fi sequence and following long s support Toxifiſaxij, correcting the OCR’s malformed Toxihſaxij.

runs.text: O que ha muitos annos que eſtà em

lines.note: Toshigoro describes someone who has been in a place for many years. The Portuguese relative clause continues below; this use differs from the age noun at the preceding column’s end.

runs.text: hua caſa, ou lugar, ou o que ha muito que ſer-

lines.note: The person has long lived in a house or place, or has long served. The scan reads lugar rather than lagar, and ſer- continues into the next row.
Ve completes serve. Toshigoro no mono is the Japanese phrase illustrating a long-established resident or long-serving person.
Toshigoto means each year. The annual sense is supplied directly by Cada anno and stands as a separate entry.

runs.text: O ir cada anno à varella, ou er-

lines.note: Toshimairi denotes making an annual visit to a shrine or hermitage. The Portuguese ermida is divided after er-.
Mida completes ermida, followed by the printed etcetera. This short line completes the annual shrine-visit definition.
Tōshin is a lamp wick. The scan supports Pauio rather than OCR Panio; torcida gives a second Portuguese word for the wick.

runs.text: diz do miolo do junco que ſerue de torcida.

lines.note: The term is specifically applied to rush pith used as a wick. This material description confirms the lexical reading of Pauio on the previous row.
Toshinami is explained by Toxinorei and glossed as the proportion or appearance of age. The synonym’s visible e corrects OCR o, while a- begins aparencia below.
Parencia completes aparencia da idade. Hatachi bakari no begins the example of someone appearing about twenty years old.
Toshinami completes the age-appearance phrase. The Portuguese repeats the age of twenty, with annos divided after an-.
Nos completes annos; pouco mais, ou menos qualifies the estimate as approximately twenty. It is a continuation of the example rather than a separate sense.
Tōshite is equated with hayō and glossed “quickly.” No final punctuation is supplied after Depreßa where the scan does not establish one.

runs.text: Cami que os gentios vão viſitar,

lines.note: Toshitoku is a kami visited by the people described in the gloss. The initial capital is T, not OCR r; Cami is embedded in Portuguese.

runs.text: ou adorar no principio do anno.

lines.note: The visit or worship occurs at the beginning of the year. This completes the description of Toshitoku.
Toshi oi means old or elderly. The Portuguese supplies the direct adjective velho without an additional example.
Toshiyori, toshiyoru, toshiyotta gives the principal forms of growing old. The printed otta preserves the inflectional pattern rather than a modernized expansion.
Toshiyori as a separate nominal entry denotes an old person. Its distinction from the preceding verb is supported by the independent headword and gloss.
Toshiyuki is assigned the same meaning by Idem, referring back to the old person in the previous entry.
Toshizakari is the prime of life. The repeated example starts with Toxizaca- and continues across the line break.

runs.text: Ser, ou eſtar na flor da idade.

lines.note: Rini naru completes toshizakari ni naru, being or reaching the prime of life. The Portuguese retains its paired ser and estar formulation.

runs.text: Lugar onde matão as vacas, ou outros

lines.note: Tosho is a place where cattle or other animals are slaughtered. The visible r in outros corrects the OCR omission.
The animals include rams and sheep. Ouelhas is one printed word, not the OCR’s artificial oue lhas division.
Tōsho means this place, kono tokoro. The Portuguese gives this place or settlement, with povoação divided after po-.
Uoação completes povoação. The visible ç and continuous word fragment correct the OCR’s spaced uo ação.
Tōshoku denotes a current superior’s office or superintendency. The Portuguese superintendente is divided at the line break.

runs.text: dente que agora corre, ou deſte tempo.

lines.note: Dente completes superintendente. The temporal qualification explains that it is the office currently held or belonging to this time.
Tōshū refers to those of this sect or religion. The two carons are retained independently, including the mark over u.
Tōshun is this spring, explained by ataru haru. The printed f of faru is partly abraded but the word and gloss agree; the second seasonal gloss follows below.
Anno nouo adds “new year” to the spring definition. This is a short continuation of Tǒxun.

runs.text: O ſair do Oriente, & porſe no

lines.note: Tōshut seibot describes rising in the east and setting in the west. The scan supports porſe rather than OCR perſe; the final t spellings are retained.
Occidente completes the westward setting phrase. The final S. is the upright written-language label and is separated from the italic Portuguese.
Toshut is vomiting, explained by haki idasu. The final upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the italic gloss.

runs.text: O botar fora com força, ou ẽpuxãdo.

lines.note: Tosshut means throwing or thrusting something out forcefully. The abbreviated ẽpuxãdo is preserved without expansion.

runs.text: Caſa onde guardão aues, ou paßaros.

lines.note: Toya is a place for keeping birds. The broken initial is capital T, and the Portuguese aues and paßaros provide the enclosure’s occupants.
The additional sense is a chicken coop. The printed pilcrow introduces a second gloss within the same Toya entry.
Tōya denotes a winter night, fuyu no yo. Its circumflex is distinct from the unmarked bird-house headword immediately above.

This catchword anticipates Toyacacuya on the following page. The printed upward circumflex is retained despite the next headword’s unmarked vowel; the short, ink-heavy terminal mark remains transcribed as the baseline hyphen.
